Flaxman orcid: 0000-0001-6033-4713 corresponding: true email: abie@ihme.washington.edu affiliations: - department: Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation name: University of Washington address: "Population Health Building/Hans Rosling Center, 3980 15th Ave. NE, UW Campus Box #351615" city: Seattle region: WA postal-code: "98195" country: USA - name: Anders Alexandersson # TODO before submission: confirm affiliation wording, add full street address and ORCID affiliations: - department: Florida Cancer Data System name: University of Miami Miller School of Medicine city: Miami region: FL country: USA abstract: | **Introduction** … **Methods** … **Results** … **Conclusion** … keywords: [record linkage, entity resolution, simulated data, cancer registry, benchmark dataset, reproducibility, pseudopeople] --- ::: {.content-visible when-format="docx"} ::: {#author-block .cell execution_count=1} **Author affiliations** | **Abraham D. Flaxman** (corresponding author), ORCID 0000-0001-6033-4713 | Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington, Population Health Building/Hans Rosling Center, 3980 15th Ave. NE, UW Campus Box #351615, Seattle WA 98195, USA | Email: abie@ihme.washington.edu | **Anders Alexandersson** | Florida Cancer Data System, University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, Miami FL, USA ::: ::: ## Key Features {.unnumbered} - **What is unique:** a large, fully simulated, multi-file dataset for linking individual people, with cross-file ground truth (every record carries a `simulant_id`, so missed-match and false-match rates of any method can be computed exactly rather than estimated), designed to capture the record matching challenges faced by a Florida-scale cancer data system. - **Why created:** linkage software for cancer registries must be developed and tested on names, dates of birth, addresses and SSNs, which are exactly the identifiers that confidentiality rules prevent registries from releasing. - **Details:** a simulated Florida drawn from the 50\,518\,675 simulants recorded as residents in the simulated 2020, 2030 or 2040 censuses, including a registry stand-in of 5\,000\,002 records whose age and sex distribution is that of the cases reported by the Florida Cancer Data System, and researcher finder files of 500\,000 and 100\,001 records drawn from residents in 2040. - **Data linkage:** the larger finder file includes 100\,000 simulants in the registry and the smaller finder file includes 20\,000 simulants. There is no overlap between the finder files. - **Main categories of data:** simulated person-level identifiers including name, date of birth, sex, street-address fields, SSN, race/ethnicity, and a diagnosis date on each registry record, carrying realistic synthetic noise (typos, nicknames, month/day swaps, blanks, duplications). - **Access:** direct download under a permissive licence with a DOI. # Background {#sec-background} … # Methods {#sec-methods} ## Generating simulated records with pseudopeople ::: {.cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pseudopeople as psp census = psp.generate_decennial_census() # bundled ~10k-simulant sample census.head() ``` ::: {#sample-demo .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: # Results {#sec-results} ## Structure, contents, and where the data are held {#sec-structure} The resource is three comma-separated files, deposited on Zenodo under a DOI that will be minted at acceptance and described in @tbl-release: a simulated registry file of 5\,000\,000 simulated people and two finder files of 500\,000 and 100\,000 simulated people respectively. All three are drawn from Florida residents in the simulated 2020, 2030 or 2040 census, a pool of 50\,518\,675 distinct simulants. Every row carries a `simulant_id`, the identifier of the simulated person it describes, and the same identifier means the same person in all three files; this is the ground truth against which any linkage of the files can be scored. The remaining fields are the ones a linkage runs on: first name, middle initial, last name, date of birth, sex, race/ethnicity, street number, street name, unit number, city, state, ZIP code and SSN. Registry rows also carry a diagnosis date, which falls in 2020, 2030 or 2040. Addresses are Florida addresses down to city and ZIP code, with simulated rather than real streets. The registry has 5\,000\,002 rows for its 5\,000\,000 people, and the finder files have 500\,000 and 100\,001 rows for 500\,000 and 100\,000 people; the few people with two rows are duplicated records (@sec-methods). The larger finder file shares 100\,000 people with the registry, 20% of its records, and the smaller shares 20\,000, the same share; the two finder files share no people with each other. Because the key is exact, every finder record is either a true match to one registry person or a true non-match, and the 100\,000 and 20\,000 true record pairs are known rather than estimated. Alongside the files, the deposit carries a manifest of MD5 and SHA-256 digests (@tbl-release gives the MD5) and the configuration file that names every seed and design target, and the pipeline that built them is archived under its own DOI . A second build from that configuration reproduced all three files byte for byte. ::: {#tbl-release .cell tbl-cap='The released files: rows, people, people shared with the registry, size and MD5 digest.
